soil-class-081.title: Tropical peat, built from fallen trees
soil-class-081.text: Tropical peat covers about 380,000 km², roughly 0.25% of Earth's land, yet it holds 50,000–70,000 million tonnes of carbon, about 3% of the carbon in the world's soils. It is a Histosol of tropical latitudes, found in South East Asia, Africa and Central and South America. Temperate peat is typically built of sphagnum, but tropical peat forms mostly from dead trees. Its organic matter content usually exceeds 75%, and its dry bulk density is low. About 46% of its area is in South America, though the world's largest tropical peat deposit lies in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The forests growing on this peat yield timber, bark, resins and latex, and they shelter endangered species such as the orangutan. Clear the forest and drain the peat, and the surface peat oxidizes, losing carbon rapidly as CO2. The sinking ground then floods. Plantations, logging and fire are shrinking the store, and Indonesia's burning peat bogs contain more than 50 billion tonnes of carbon. Leaving these emissions out underestimates the rise in greenhouse gases and human-induced climate change.

soil-class-055.title: Who made terra preta, and how
soil-class-055.text: Early theories traced them to ashfall from Andean volcanoes, or to sediment settling in ancient lakes or ponds. Sources still differ. Some terra preta was clearly made on purpose. Much may have built up by accident, since soil rich in charcoal and pottery gathers near dwellings. Many patches probably formed under kitchen middens, or refuse heaps. Recent research suggests terra preta may even be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility. The soils vary so much that it remains unclear whether all were made deliberately, or whether the lightest are by-products of daily life.

soil-class-056.title: Recreating Amazonian dark soil
soil-class-056.text: Synthetic terra preta is a {{ref:soil-fert-001}} made from materials meant to copy those of the original: crushed clay, blood and ground bone, animal dung and charcoal made for soil. Because it is particulate, it can move down the soil profile and add fertility and carbon to existing peds and aggregates. Poor tropical soils can also be enriched to terra preta nova by adding charcoal and condensed smoke. It might lock away carbon while reversing declining fertility and the spread of desert, but whether this works at large scale is unproven. A related idea, terra preta sanitation, pairs lactic-acid treatment in urine-diverting dry toilets with worms that break down the waste.

soil-class-058.title: Red soil, the iron-stained clay of warm lands
soil-class-058.text: About 13% of Earth's soil is red. Red soil is a reddish, clay-rich soil that typically develops in warm, temperate and humid climates, usually from weathered ancient crystalline and metamorphic rock. Thin, heavily leached organic layers rest on a red layer of river-laid sediment. High iron gives colors from reddish brown to reddish yellow, and Ultisols, Alfisols and Oxisols count as red soil once they take on this color. No single composition defines the group: one type may be infertile in one region but rich in nutrients in another. Heavy leaching leaves them acidic and low in water-holding capacity, nutrients and humus. Nitrogen is often deficient, and phosphorus and potassium run short after repeated harvests. Adding lime raises their pH for acid-intolerant crops, though it can stimulate microbes that deplete organic matter and harm structure. Organic matter added as dung, suitable cultivation and changing crops from year to year raise fertility and water retention. Red soils cover about 102 million hectares in China and about 350,000 km², 10.6% of the country, in India.

soil-class-085.title: Bay mud, the soft floor of estuaries
soil-class-085.text: Bay mud is thick deposits of soft, water-saturated, loose silty clay on the floors of certain estuaries, mostly in temperate regions shaped by glacial cycles. Tributary streams wash in its clay, silt and sand. It has low shear strength, high compressibility and low permeability, with a typical bulk density of about 1.3 g/cm³. That makes it hazardous to build on in earthquake zones such as San Francisco Bay. Heavy buildings need deep foundations on stiffer layers below, and even then the ground around them settles, damaging utility connections. At low tide it forms mudflats that feed shorebirds and root eelgrass, cordgrass and pickleweed.

soil-class-049.title: Brown podzolic soils, halfway between two kinds
soil-class-049.text: Brown podzolic soils are a class of the British soil classification, grouped with the podzolic soils but halfway between a Podzol and a brown earth. They form on hilly land in western Europe. There, more than about 900 mm of precipitation outstrips evaporation for much of the year, so the profile is leached. Unlike true podzols, they lack a continuous E horizon. Soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminum oxides, which build up as a distinctive orange-brown B horizon. The WRB calls them Umbrisols. They are common in Ireland, Scotland, western England and Wales, where they cover about 20% of the country.

soil-class-065.title: Brickearth, the wind-blown silt of southern England
soil-class-065.text: Brickearth is a superficial deposit of uniform loam or silt, first named in southern England, and it is wind-blown loess. In the cold, dry periods of the Pleistocene, wind picked up fine sediment from glacial outwash and dropped it where the wind slackened. It lies in patchy spreads up to a meter deep across southern England and South Wales. With little or no added material it makes stock bricks, which harden at lower temperatures than clay bricks. It gives rich farmland, but it collapses rapidly when saturated and makes a poor foundation.

soil-class-064.title: Stagnogley, the waterlogged soil over a dense layer
soil-class-064.text: Stagnogley is a loamy or clayey soil with a dense, impervious horizon beneath the surface, classed among the gleyic soils. Continual waterlogging bleaches its topsoil, and it often forms on sandy material over dense subsoil in cool, moist climates. Nutrient-poor, often highly acidic and poorly aerated, it suits woodland such as English oak better than crops. Where it stays saturated all year it becomes bog stagnogley and eventually bog, as in the missen of the Black Forest. Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in very humid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

soil-class-068.title: Subaqueous soil, soil beneath the water
soil-class-068.text: Soil does not stop at the shoreline. Subaqueous soil forms in the sediment of shallow, permanently flooded places, or anywhere under water too deep for rooted plants. These sediments undergo soil-forming processes and can support rooted plants such as eelgrass. They also meet the definition of soil in {{ref:soil-class-006}}, opening a new frontier for {{ref:soil-agri-082}}. They differ from submerged soils, which formed on land and were later flooded by rising water tables, beaver dams or sea level rise. Subaqueous soils formed under a continuous water column, as in an estuary. The US concept arose only in the early 1990s. George Demas pioneered it in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay. He saw that these areas supported rooted plants and had formed horizons. Survey inventories use an arbitrary water depth limit of 2.5 m, which some states have extended to 5 m. Treating them as soils lets scientists trace linked horizons across the underwater landscape, aiding seagrass restoration.

soil-class-086.title: Calcareous grassland, the grazed turf of chalk downs
soil-class-086.text: Calcareous grassland, also called alkaline grassland, grows on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, where shallow soils like {{ref:soil-class-050}} are common. Large areas occur in northwestern Europe, especially on Salisbury Plain and the North and South Downs of England. Machair is a variant on calcium-rich shell sand. Short, hardy grasses and herbs such as clover dominate, held at a plagioclimax, a stage fixed by sheep or cattle grazing. It is an important habitat for insects, particularly butterflies and ants. Its lichens, favored by stable flints and nutrient-poor soil, have declined since the mid-20th century through reduced grazing, nitrogen settling from the air and habitat loss.

soil-class-067.title: Takir, the bare clay flats of Central Asia
soil-class-067.text: In the deserts of Central Asia, seasonal rain floods shallow hollows of heavy clay soil. When the water evaporates, it leaves a takir: a smooth, bare clay flat, similar to a salt flat. The Turkic name means 'smooth, even, or bare'. A dried, fissured crust forms on the surface, often colonized by threadlike cyanobacteria. Similar flats are called playas or salt flats in the southwestern United States and sabkha in Arab countries. Calcisols were formerly known internationally as Desert soils and Takyrs.

soil-class-062.title: Serpentine barrens, grassland where forest should be
soil-class-062.text: Where the climate should grow forest, serpentine rock can hold open grassland instead. Serpentine barrens are grassland or savanna on serpentine outcrops, an ecoregion in parts of the United States. They are likeliest where the ultramafic rock never received richer sediment carried by water, glaciers or wind, such as loess, sand or volcanic ash. They occur in small patches of the Appalachians and the Pacific Coast Ranges. Grazing them is risky: one study found toxic nickel in the kidneys of 20% of grazing animals and toxic copper in the livers of 32%. Fire suppression turned Pennsylvania's Rock Springs barren into forest, while controlled burns since 1995 have restored sparse species at Buck Creek, North Carolina.

soil-class-061.title: The tough, rare plants of serpentine soils
soil-class-061.text: In California, 10% of the state's plants are serpentine endemics, found only on these soils. Serpentine plant communities are marked by poor productivity, many such endemics, and tolerance of drought, heavy metals and scarce nutrients. Low calcium-to-magnesium ratios limit root growth and nutrient uptake, while heavy metals stunt growth and yellow the leaves. Plants respond with deep roots, by excluding or storing metals, or by tolerating them. Many are stunted, with dull, waxy gray-green leaves that hold water and reflect sunlight. Tolerance has evolved many times, and patchy, isolated habitats limit gene flow and promote new species. In California 45% of serpentine-associated taxa are rare or endangered.

soil-class-087.title: Blue goo, the clay that slides off California hills
soil-class-087.text: Blue goo is a sticky, plastic, bluish-gray clay soil formed from highly weathered serpentinite mélange, a jumble of sheared rocks. Its source is the Franciscan Complex: greenstones, cherts, basalts, shales, sandstones, schists and serpentinites sheared between the Pacific and North American plates. Gleying without oxygen gives the color, and a grayer variant is called grey goo. The clay holds much water and drains poorly. Saturated, it slips, especially in shallow soils under heavy rain, feeding {{ref:soil-water-057}} on the Northern California coast. It has been found only in the Trinidad and Orick regions of Humboldt County, California.

soil-class-063.title: Duplex soils, sand over clay in Australia
soil-class-063.text: Duplex soil is an Australian term for a soil with a sharp contrast in texture between its horizons. In Northcote's Factual Key, the B horizon is at least one and a half texture classes finer than the A horizon. The change is clear to sharp, within 0.1 m. Topsoils range from coarse sand to clay loam, subsoils from light to heavy clay, and some have a bleached A2 horizon. Northcote used color to separate brown, red and yellow duplex soils. The Australian Soil Classification spreads them among Podosols, Sodosols, Chromosols and Kurosols. Similar soils in strongly seasonal climates such as the Mediterranean are called calcic and chromic Luvisols.

soil-class-052.title: Where terra rossa came from: three rival answers
soil-class-052.text: What is terra rossa made of? Geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists have long argued over its origin and its link to the carbonate rock beneath, and they still disagree. One group holds that it is insoluble residue: sediment and chert left concentrated as the underlying carbonate rocks dissolved. Another says residue alone cannot explain it. In this view the soil is polygenetic, formed by more than one process, with parent material that includes volcanic ash and non-carbonate or wind-blown sediment, depending on location. A third group proposes metasomatic replacement, the chemical swapping of one rock's minerals for others.

soil-class-059.title: Latosol, the deep red soil of the rainforest
soil-class-059.text: Latosols can reach 20–30 m deep, against 1–2 m for podzols. A latosol, also called tropical red earth, is a rainforest soil with a relatively high content of iron and aluminum oxides. It is usually classed as an Oxisol in USDA soil taxonomy or a Ferralsol in the WRB. Iron oxides color it red or yellowish-red throughout. A thin but very fertile humus layer from the forest above lies over an infertile layer stripped by rapid leaching under heavy rain. Fertility depends wholly on the rainforest. Once it is felled and the humus is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

soil-class-066.title: Gumbo, the clay that turns to sticky mud
soil-class-066.text: Gumbo soil is dominated by very fine clay particles, often with small amounts of sand or organic material. It holds water exceptionally well. Rain, though, turns it into a sticky mud that is hard to work with large farm machinery. Skipping the plow seems to pay: farming gumbo without plowing appears strongly linked to higher yields than traditional methods.

soil-class-082.title: Mesotrophic soil, the middle rank of fertility
soil-class-082.text: Soils can be ranked by their inherent fertility. A mesotrophic soil sits in the middle, between rich eutrophic soils and poor oligotrophic ones. One measure for placing it is base status, an indicator of fertility. Base status relates the major nutrient cations, calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium, to the soil's clay percentage. It is commonly expressed in hundredths of a mole of cations per kilogram of clay, written cmol(+) kg−1 clay.

soil-class-069.title: Mapping soils from the water
soil-class-069.text: Subaqueous soil mapping surveys underwater soils much as land soils are mapped, except that the mapper works from the water. Bathymetric maps, which chart the depth of the bottom, take the place of topographic maps and aerial photographs for identifying underwater landforms. Augers with extendable shafts, peat corers and vibracores replace shovels for sampling. Several US states have begun the work, each NRCS state office setting its priority by local conservation concerns. Interpretations for different uses are still being developed and should grow as more areas are surveyed.

reviews.other-soil-types: Peat runs through much of this chapter: partly decayed plants that pile up where waterlogging stalls decay, storing up to 550 Gt of carbon on just 3% of the land, then releasing it when drained, burned or thawed. Rewetting, by blocking drainage channels, lets damaged bogs begin to rebuild that store. Other soils here are named for their rock, from metal-laden serpentine soils and the sliding blue goo to rendzinas and terra rossa on limestone. People made some of them, from Amazonian terra preta, rich in charcoal that lasts thousands of years, to the dark earth of old towns and the fill that raised Kansai's airport island. Still others are defined by climate or water, from the brown earths of temperate Europe and the red soils that make up about 13% of Earth's soil to subaqueous soils beneath shallow estuaries.
